THOUGHT: This is a chronic (5-year) poikilodermatous eruption of flexural skin (axillae, groin, flanks) with mildly pruritic hypopigmented/hyperpigmented reticulated patches and thin atrophic plaques. Histology shows epidermotropism of atypical lymphocytes with convoluted nuclei and a superficial perivascular/interstitial T‑cell infiltrate. Immunophenotype is T‑cell (CD3+) with loss of CD7, no B‑cell (CD20) or CD30 population, and a CD8 > CD4 predominance. T‑cell clonality studies are negative. Key points favoring a cutaneous T‑cell lymphoma (CTCL)/mycosis fungoides (MF) picture: chronicity, poikilodermatous clinical pattern, epidermotropism, cytologically atypical lymphocytes, loss of the pan‑T marker CD7. The negative TCR clonality does not exclude early MF (clonality can be undetectable in patch/early disease). Although classic MF is often CD4+, CD8‑predominant MF and other CD8+ CTCL variants are well‑described. Alternative diagnoses to consider are inflammatory/parapsoriatic disorders that can mimic MF histologically (large‑plaque parapsoriasis / parapsoriasis variegata — often considered an MF precursor), pityriasis lichenoides, chronic eczematous/lichenoid dermatitis, and rarer CD8+ primary cutaneous cytotoxic lymphomas (more aggressive and usually clinically distinct). Lymphomatoid papulosis and CD30+ lymphomas are unlikely given negative CD30. Connective‑tissue poikiloderma (e.g., dermatomyositis/lupus) is less likely given the histology and lack of systemic signs.

DIAGNOSIS:
1. Mycosis fungoides — poikilodermatous/patch‑stage CTCL (CD8‑predominant variant)
2. Large‑plaque parapsoriasis / parapsoriasis variegata (early MF spectrum)
3. Chronic eczematous/dermatitic process (inverse/flexural eczema with atypical reactive lymphocytes)
4. Pityriasis lichenoides chronica (PLC) / pityriasis lichenoides spectrum
5. Primary cutaneous CD8+ epidermotropic cytotoxic T‑cell lymphoma (rare/aggressive CD8+ CTCL variant)

Case Information:
A man in his 40s with a 5-year history of mildly pruritic poikilodermatous patches and thin plaques involving the bilateral axilla and groin presented with expanding lesions on both flanks. He had not received any prior treatment for the lesions. Review of systems was unremarkable.

Physical Examination:
There were hypopigmented and hyperpigmented reticulated patches and thin, atrophic plaques covering more than 10% of the total body surface area involving the axilla, groin, and flanks bilaterally. No cervical, axillary, or inguinal lymphadenopathy was noted.

Diagnostic Tests:
